title: Ki Tavo: coming in, going out (Deuteronomy 28:3–6)
hookLine: blessed in the city and the field, coming in and going out
tomorrow: Ki Tavo: a heart to know (Deuteronomy 29:3)

cards: Count how many thresholds you'll cross today. Out the front door. Into a car or onto a bus.
Into work, or school, or a store. Back out. Back home.

Most of those crossings take less than a second and leave no memory at all. On the doorframe of a Jewish home there's a small case, a mezuzah, and some people touch it as they pass, going in and going out.
The doorway is treated as a place worth a moment. Today's verses bless exactly those crossings, and everything around them.

teach.h: IN THE CITY, IN THE FIELD.
teach.b: Deuteronomy twenty-eight opens with a list of blessings, if the people keep the covenant. It starts small and wide at once: "Blessed shalt thou be in the city, and blessed shalt thou be in the field."

Then the children and the herds, the basket and the kneading-trough. And it ends: "Blessed shalt thou be when thou comest in, and blessed shalt thou be when thou goest out." City and field cover where you are.

Coming in and going out cover how you move between them. Hardly a moment of the day is left out. The basket and the kneading-trough are kitchen things, where the bread begins; the blessing reaches right into the bowl.
The Talmud, in Bava Metzia, gives the last verse a second reading.

teach.h: ARRIVING IN, AND LEAVING, THE WORLD.
teach.b: Coming in and going out can mean coming into the world and leaving it: may your leaving be like your arriving, free of wrongdoing. A whole life read as one doorway.
A psalm uses the same pair: "The LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in, from this time forth and for ever."
These blessings sit in a hard chapter.
They're short, and the curses that follow are long and frightening; by custom the reader chants those quickly and in a lowered voice.
But the chapter begins with blessing, and the blessing is about the plainest movements a person makes.

how: Some Jews touch the mezuzah on the doorframe when entering and leaving a home, and some say Psalm 121, with its line about going out and coming in, before a journey.

o: when you lie down, a phrase from the evening prayers
when you come in, the phrase that names this portion
when you give, a phrase from the laws of tithes

games.q: where the blessing reaches — tap the pairs.
p: leave the world as you entered it

s: the blessings in Deuteronomy 28 are longer than the curses
the blessings are short; the curses after them are long.
the Talmud reads coming in and going out as entering and leaving the world
the same pair, going out and coming in, appears in a psalm

games.q: you're the Torah reader in synagogue, and you've reached the long curses of chapter 28. what does custom say?
o: chant them quickly, in a lowered voice.
games.why: they're read, not skipped, but quickly and quietly, while the blessings that open the chapter are read in full voice.

practice: Picture the door you'll walk out of next, your hand on it, and a half-second pause before you go through.
If you pray, the psalm's words are there: the LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in; if you don't, a breath and a wish that the day goes well will do.
Then picture coming back through the same door tonight, and pausing there too.

wordCard.voice: Ki Tavo. When you come in. The portion where blessing covers the city and the field, the coming in and the going out.

orig.note: Hebrew: blessed are you in your coming in. Deuteronomy 28:6.

carryVoice: Your line: blessed coming and going. Even the kneading bowl gets a blessing. That's day five hundred fifteen.

sources.q: Blessed shalt thou be in the city, and blessed shalt thou be in the field.
Blessed shalt thou be when thou comest in, and blessed shalt thou be when thou goest out.
